readings.c3s2:
¶
'''transpalatine''' (trȧns-pal′a̤-tin), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''trans-'' + ''palatine''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Transverse, as a palatine bone which extends on either side from the median line.

'''II.''' ''n.'' The transpalatine bone of certain sauropsidan vertebrates.

'''transpalmar''' (trȧns-pal′mär), ''a.'' [< L. ''trans'', across, + ''palma'', palm: see ''palm''<sup>1</sup>, ''palmar''.] Situated across the palm of the hand; lying crosswise in the palm.—{{smaller|'''Transpalmar muscle''', the transpalmaris.}}

'''transpalmaris''' (trȧns-pal-mā′ris), ''n.''; pl. ''transpalmares'' (-rēz). [NL.: see ''transpalmar''.] The transpalmar muscle of the hand; the palmaris brevis. See ''palmaris''. ''Coues'', 1887.

'''transpanamic''' (trȧns-pa-nam′ik), ''a.'' [< ''trans-'' + ''Panama'' (see def.) + ''-ic''.] Existing or located on the other side of the Isthmus of Panama from the position of the speaker. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The Formicariidæ . . . thin out very much in the ''Transpanamic'' subregion on the north.
{{right|''P. L. Sclater'', Cat. Birds Brit. Mus., XV. 176.}}}}

'''transpare†''' (trans-pãr′), ''v. i.'' [= It. ''trasparere'', ''trasparire'', < ML. ''transparere'', shine through, < L. ''trans'', through, + ''parere'', appear: see ''appear''.] To appear through something else; be visible through something.

{{smaller block|But through the yce of that vniust disdaine,
Yet still ''transpares'' her picture and my paine.
{{right|''Stirling'', Aurora, Sonnet xcix.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''transparence''' (trans-pãr′e̤ns), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''transparance''; < F. ''transparence'' = Sp. ''transparencia'', ''trasparencia'' = Pg. ''transparencia'' = It. ''trasparenzia'', ''trasparenza'', < ML. ''transparentia'', < ''transparen''(''t''-)''s'', transparent: see ''transparent''.] Same as ''transparency''.

{{smaller block|(The casements standing wide)
Clearely through that ''transparance'' is espy'de
This Glutton, whom they by his habit knew.
{{right|''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 575.}}}}

{{smaller block|But breezes played, and sunshine gleamed, . . .
Reddened the fiery hues, and shot
''Transparence'' through the golden.
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Yarrow Revisited.}}}}

'''transparency''' (trȧns-pãr′en-si), ''n.'' [As ''transparence'' (see ''-cy'').] 1. The property or state of being transparent; that state or property of a body by which it admits of the passage of rays of light so that forms, colors, and brightness of objects can be seen through it; diaphaneity.

{{smaller block|The clearness and ''transparency'' of the stream.
{{right|''Addison'', Remarks on Italy (ed. Bohn, I. 367).}}}}

{{smaller block|Their silver wings flashing in the pure ''transparency'' of the air.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Marble Faun, vi.}}}}

2. Something intended to be seen by means of transmitted light, as a picture, a sign, or other representation; often, an announcement of news, painted on canvas or other translucent material and lighted from behind; hence, by extension, a frame or construction, usually of wood and muslin, containing the lights necessary, and having one, two, or four inscriptions, or the like, on different sides.

readings.c4s3:
¶

{{smaller block|This fell tempest shall not cease to rage
Until the golden circuit on my head,
Like to the glorious sun's ''transparent'' beams,
Do calm the fury of this mad-bred flaw.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 353.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Transparent colors''', in ''painting'', colors such as will transmit light, or so delicately or thinly laid on as to veil without concealing the ground or other colors behind them: opposed to ''opaque colors'', which only reflect light; also, colors which appear only by transmitted light, as those of stained glass, which, as correctly conceived, should be wholly transparent and with no opaque shadows.—'''Transparent corpuscles of Norris''', colorless bodies found in the blood, supposed to be decolorized red blood-corpuscles.—'''Transparent gold ocher.''' See ''ocher''.—'''Transparent lacquer, leather, soap.''' See the nouns.—'''Transparent oxid of chromium.''' See ''chromium''. ='''Syn.''' 1. Bright, limpid, crystalline.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A costume consisting of a dress of lace, tulle, gauze, or other thin fabric, worn over another dress of rich material. This fashion seems to have been introduced about 1675.

'''transparently''' (trâns-pãr′ent-li), ''adv.'' In a transparent manner; so as to be seen through; clearly.

'''transparentness''' (trȧns-pãr′ẹnt-nes), ''n.'' The property or state of being transparent; transparency; diaphaneity.

'''transpass†''' (trȧns-pȧs′), ''v.'' [< ML. ''transpassare'', pass over, < L. ''trans'', over, + ML. ''passare'', pass: see ''pass''. Cf. ''trespass'', an older form of the same word.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To pass over.

{{smaller block|The river Hyphasis, or, as Ptolemy calleth it, Bipasis, was Alexander's non ultra; which yet he ''transpassed'', and set up altars on the other side.
{{right|''Gregory'', Notes on Scripture, p. 75. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To pass by or away.

{{right|''Daniel'', Description of Beauty.}}}}
